subject: Biology
title: Seagrass Meadows
description: A micro-lesson that makes Seagrass Meadows usable.

hook.text: Seagrass is the only flowering plant that lives entirely underwater. It even pollinates in the current.

buildup.text: Seagrass meadows stabilize sediment, filter water, and provide nursery habitat for young fish.

discovery.text: One square meter of seagrass can produce 10 liters of oxygen per day through photosynthesis.

twist.text: Seagrass captures carbon 35 times faster than tropical rainforests per unit area.

climax.text: An estimated 7% of seagrass is lost worldwide each year—faster than tropical forests are disappearing.

punchline.text: The ocean's most underrated ecosystem. Vanishing quietly.

quiz.question: How does seagrass compare to rainforests in carbon capture?
options: It captures carbon 35 times faster per unit area

details.summary: Seagrass meadows are underwater flowering plants that form extensive meadows in shallow coastal waters worldwide. They stabilize sediments, nurture juvenile fish, and store carbon up to 35 times faster than tropical rainforests per unit area, making them vital blue carbon ecosystems.
details.whyItMatters: Seagrass meadows are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth yet are disappearing at alarming rates. Their carbon storage capacity means that protecting seagrass is both a biodiversity conservation and climate change strategy.
takeaways: Seagrass stores carbon 35 times faster per hectare than tropical rainforest
Meadows are nursery habitat for commercially important fish and shellfish
Seagrass is disappearing at a rate of about 7 percent per year globally

faq.question: Why is seagrass so effective at storing carbon?
faq.answer: Seagrass traps sediment particles and dead organic matter within its root systems and surrounding sediment. The low-oxygen conditions in these sediments prevent decomposition, locking carbon away for centuries to millennia. The dense root network accelerates sediment burial.

faq.question: What is causing seagrass decline?
faq.answer: Coastal development, pollution, and nutrient runoff cause algal blooms that block light. Dredging and boat anchoring physically destroy meadows. Climate change warms waters beyond tolerance. These combined threats have destroyed an estimated 29 percent of global seagrass since 1879.
